# Whose verdict counts? Synthetic and recorded GNSS interference for a robot integrity monitor

Status: generated draft. Simulation numbers are SYNTHETIC. Every number is filled by `docsgen/facts.py` from the data files; text edits go in `docs/templates/MANUSCRIPT.tmpl.md`. The recorded arm has not been run (see the section on round three), so this draft answers the first half of the research question only. Single author, no human check of the evidence table yet, no outside reader yet.

## Abstract

Where no instrument fixes the conditions a service robot must be shown safe under, the developer's own simulation becomes the evidence. We build a source traced table of 222 rows over 24 instrument families and measure its extraction error (either pass, 32.0 percent, interval 26.2 to 38.4 percent). We audit 38 in scope rows for what they leave to the developer: of 12 that ask for environmental or interference evidence, 0 fix a severity and 0 fix one that applies to a Gulf site. We encode published simulation credibility conditions in a checker for a machine readable assurance case, so that 21 evidence items each carry a ceiling on the claim they can support. Two preregistered synthetic rounds hit 21 of 23 and 17 of 19 predictions; a mutation audit of the predictions found n/a uninformative (round three state: not yet run). All simulated evidence is synthetic, written by the authors of the monitors it tests, and supports no claim about a real robot.

## Introduction

A team that builds a safety monitor also builds the simulation that tests it. If the regulation is silent on which conditions count, that simulation is the evidence. The question is whether such evidence agrees with what happens on recorded data, and whether credibility conditions that already exist in other fields would have warned us. The study makes four contributions: the evidence table, the silence audit, a checker that applies credibility conditions to an assurance case and keeps hardware claims open, and a preregistered design for comparing synthetic with recorded interference. It does not propose a new credibility framework, a safety case for a real robot or any legal conclusion.

## Related work

Credibility of simulation as evidence is treated by risk based frameworks, a ladder of simulator admissibility, the NASA credibility scale and guidance on independence of verification. These are listed with their status in `docs/RELATED_WORK.md` and `data/related_work.csv`; abstracts and page summaries were read, not all originals, and paywalled standards were not read. We adopt their conditions and encode them. The open piece is a verdict comparison on one monitor with thresholds fixed in advance.

## Evidence table

The table has 222 rows. Access level: full text seen 41, summary seen 167, title only 14. Binding status: mandatory 43, conditional 56, voluntary 48, guidance 75. A second and third pass measured the error rate in a sample: 32.0 percent of rows had an error in either pass, 95 percent interval 26.2 to 38.4 percent. Rows changed by the final check had 32.9 percent further errors, and unchanged rows 20.0 percent. A human check of a stratified sample of sixty rows is designed (`data/human_check/DESIGN.md`) and has not been done; until it is, the error rates come from automated passes of one model family.

## Silence audit

Two automated coders, instances of one model family, coded 54 candidate rows with a written codebook (`data/silence_audit/CODEBOOK.md`). Cohen's kappa by field ranged from 0.67 to 0.92. After resolving disagreements, 38 rows were in scope and 16 out of scope. Of the in scope rows, 12 ask for evidence, 16 do not, and 10 are unclear. Among those that ask, 1 fix a test method, 0 fix a severity, 0 fix a severity that applies to a Gulf site, and 6 leave the conditions to the developer. Restricting to the 9 rows seen as full text, 1 leave conditions to the developer. Limit: Applies to retrieved text only. Two automated coders of one model family; agreement does not remove shared error. Rows seen as summary or title only cannot show that an instrument is silent.

## Assurance case and credit ledger

The library robot case has 10 goals and 21 evidence items: 16 open, 5 partial and 0 provided. The checker gives each item a ceiling (none, demonstration, indicative, supporting) from four conditions it can verify by opening a referenced file: stated context of use, validation against measured data, reported sensitivity or uncertainty, and a verifier record showing independence. A hardware claim also needs bench or field evidence. Today the partial items are EV-08 (simulated, `sim/results/EV-08.json`), EV-12 (simulated, `sim/results/EV-12.json`), EV-19 (simulated, `sim/results_r2/EV-19.json`), EV-20 (simulated, `sim/results_r2/EV-20.json`), EV-21 (simulated, `sim/results_r2/EV-21.json`); goals resting on simulation alone are G1, G4, G6. The checker reports 0 errors and 56 flags.

## Simulation rounds one and two

Round one (preregistration SHA-256 `f1e6fb576949358faf5dfe3d8233f1c4da2b2e4103d5281ec3029bce616e2095`): 21 of 23 predictions hit; missed N-P4, N-P8. Criteria held AC-DU1, AC-DU2, AC-N2; failed AC-GL1, AC-GL2, AC-N1. Round two (SHA-256 `0d391addddbd7ff14eab2d828364a5339db8f1b4002c25cf18282f3d1d3fb925`): 17 of 19 predictions hit; missed GL3R2-P1, H-P2; criteria failed AC-GL1R2, AC-DU1R2, AC-DU2R2, AC-H1, AC-H3, AC-N1R2, AC-N2R2. The detail is in `docs/EVALUATION.md` and `docs/EVALUATION_R2.md`.

## Round three

Informativeness audit (state: not yet run). A prediction is informative if its verdict changes under any of four classes of mutant: a monitor that never alarms, one that alarms at once, each assumed parameter scaled by one half and by one and a half, and a shifted fault onset. Across n/a mutant runs, n/a of n/a predictions were informative, and n/a of those hit, against n/a hits overall. Uninformative predictions: n/a.

Second author generator. A second generator was written in a fresh context from a written specification (`docs/INDEPENDENT_GENERATOR_SPEC.md`). Across 6 compared verdicts, 0 differ. Limit: Same model family as the first author, so errors can repeat. The spec fixes the central error values, so this tests the implementation and its reading of the fault classes, not the choice of those values.

Recorded arm. Not run. It requires registration of the design and a licence entry for the data; the harness and its tests exist on synthetic fixtures only (`sim/r3/recorded.py`).

## Discussion

What can be said now is narrow. The checker keeps hardware claims open for every item whose evidence is simulated, and the mutation audit shows how much of the earlier hit rate could not have failed. Whether a developer written generator and recorded interference give the same verdict is not answered here, because the recorded arm has not been run.

## Threats to validity

Single author. Checkers and coders share a model family with the author, so errors can repeat. Parameters are assumed, not measured. Standards were read at summary level where only summaries were available. Recordings, when used, may not come from the Gulf. See `docs/LIMITATIONS.md`. Official items: 71 checked against official texts by an automated service, of which 34 are not confirmed and need hand reading (`docs/FETCH_LIST_R3.md`).
